Naveen had eleven minutes to buy the vegetables and get back, because his wife Hansa had said forty minutes and it had already been twenty-nine. The queue at the sabzi stall wasn't moving.
His phone buzzed. Where are you? Then: Who are you talking to?
There was nobody to show the screen to. He hadn't been to Friday cricket in eight months, or called his school friend Mahesh since March, because the last call had made Hansa cry all night.
He had started asking before every small thing. Can I buy the cheaper soap? Can I visit Amma on Sunday? Each answer came with a look he had learned to read carefully.
A man in the queue was grumbling loudly about his wife's nagging. Naveen almost laughed. What he lived with had no name he could say out loud. Nobody had ever hit him. So it couldn't be that bad, could it?
He paid, forgot the coriander, and ran.

qa.q: How long had Hansa given Naveen for the errand?
qa.a: Hansa had said forty minutes.

qa.q: Why does Naveen tell himself it couldn't be that bad?
qa.a: Because nobody had ever hit him, he doubts his own harm, even though he lives with fear and constant checking.

qa.q: What small, safe step could help Naveen?
qa.a: He could quietly reach out to someone he trusts, like Mahesh or Amma, or a support helpline, to talk about what is happening and learn his options.

qa.q: What would change if Naveen could name what he lives with?
qa.a: Naming it as control could help him see the harm as real and seek support, instead of dismissing it because there are no bruises.

grounding: A man whose wife tracks his time, contacts and small choices feels he walks on eggshells, and doubts it counts as harm because there are no bruises.

"What do you do on weekends these days?" Radhika from accounts asked, as they waited for the lift in the office tower.
Chetan opened his mouth and found nothing. He used to play in a Sunday band. He used to eat biryani with his college gang every month. Now weekends belonged to Nitin: Nitin's plans, Nitin's friends, Nitin checking the grocery bill line by line.
"Oh, you know. Quiet," he said.
In the lift he sent the usual message, because Nitin liked to know: Leaving at 6:10. He noticed he had already planned his route to avoid the lane where Nitin once saw him talking to a coworker and then didn't speak to him for two days.
No shouting, no marks. Just a thousand small permissions. Chetan wondered when he had stopped thinking of his life as his own. Before the lift doors opened, he saved Radhika's number.

qa.q: What did Chetan use to do on Sundays?
qa.a: He used to play in a Sunday band.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when Radhika asked about weekends?
qa.a: He felt blank and a little ashamed, suddenly seeing how little of his own life was left.

qa.q: Why might saving Radhika's number matter?
qa.a: It is a small step back towards his own connections; people outside can later help him reach support or a helpline safely.

qa.q: How might Radhika see Chetan's answer "Quiet"?
qa.a: Radhika may sense something in the pause, but without knowing more might simply think Chetan likes calm weekends.

grounding: A young man realises his weekends, friends and routes are all arranged around Nitin's rules, and that the harm is real even without shouting or marks.

passage:
At the insurance office where she'd worked for two years, Sharmila used to be the one who organised birthday lunches. Now, when colleagues asked her to join, she said, "I'll check," and then didn't come.
On Thursday, the team lead asked her to travel to Nashik for a client meeting. Sharmila said, "Can I tell you tomorrow?" She needed to ask Vikas first. She always needed to ask Vikas first: about lunches, about late meetings, about which colleagues she spoke to.
In the washroom, she stood at the sink and realised her hands were shaking. Over a simple work trip.
There were no bruises. Vikas never hit her. So she had never called it anything. But she walked on eggshells every evening, and her world was now her desk, her home, and his rules.
A colleague came in, saw her face and said softly, "Sharmila, are you okay?" For the first time, Sharmila said, "No. Not really."

qa.q: Where was the client meeting Sharmila was asked to travel to?
qa.a: In Nashik.

qa.q: What was Sharmila feeling at the washroom sink?
qa.a: Sharmila felt anxious and shaken, her hands trembling over a simple work trip, realising how much she lived on eggshells.

qa.q: What small step at the end could lead to help?
qa.a: Admitting to a colleague that she was not okay could open the way to talking to someone and getting support.

qa.q: How might the colleague see the change in Sharmila?
qa.a: The colleague may have noticed Sharmila withdrawing from lunches and trips, and feel concerned enough to ask gently.

grounding: It shows an adult whose world has shrunk to checking every choice with her husband, not calling it abuse because there are no bruises.

Dear Noor,
It's been a year since I answered your messages properly. I'm sorry. I want to explain, even though it's hard.
After the wedding, things changed slowly. First I stopped coming to our Sunday lunches because he didn't like them. Then I started asking him before I met anyone. Then before I bought anything. Now I think about how he'll react before I choose what to cook, what to wear, what to say.
He has never hit me, Noor. So for a long time I told myself this wasn't abuse. Just marriage. Just how he is.
But last week I realised I was whispering on the phone with my own mother. In my own home. I walk on eggshells all day.
I'm not asking you to fix anything. I just needed one person outside to know. Could we speak on Thursday at noon, when he's at work? I found a helpline number too. I haven't called yet.
Vandana

qa.q: When does Vandana ask to speak with Noor?
qa.a: On Thursday at noon, when he's at work.

qa.q: What is Vandana feeling as she writes the letter?
qa.a: Vandana feels ashamed and afraid, living on eggshells and unsure whether to call it abuse without any bruises.

qa.q: What small steps is Vandana taking?
qa.a: Vandana is reaching out to Noor, someone outside, and she has found a helpline number to call.

qa.q: How might Noor feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Noor would likely feel worried and relieved to hear from Vandana, and ready to listen without judging.

grounding: A letter shows an adult who has stopped seeing friends and checks every choice in advance, not calling it abuse because there are no bruises.

Arnab, you asked why I stopped coming to family dinners. I'm Lalremsiami, your sister, and I'm going to try to say it without crying.
It wasn't one big thing. It was small things. He didn't like my friends, so I saw them less. He wanted to know where I was, so I started sending him my location. He said my laugh was embarrassing in public, so I laughed less. Now, before I buy vegetables, I think about what he'll say.
He's never hurt me. There's never been a mark. So I kept telling myself it wasn't abuse. It was just him being particular.
But last month I went to a support group at the women's centre, and a woman there described her week, and it was my week. Exactly.
My world is so small now, Arnab. I'm not asking you to do anything big. Just keep calling me. Please don't stop calling.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami go last month?
qa.a: To a support group at the women's centre.

qa.q: How does Lalremsiami feel talking to Arnab?
qa.a: Lalremsiami feels close to tears, ashamed and frightened, recognising how small and controlled her world has become.

qa.q: What has Lalremsiami already done, and what does she ask of Arnab?
qa.a: She has joined a support group, and she asks Arnab to keep calling her, not to do anything big.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel hearing this?
qa.a: Arnab would likely feel worried and sad, and perhaps want to act, though his sister asks only that he keep calling.

grounding: An adult tells her brother how her world shrank through small controls with no marks, and why she had not called it abuse.

passage:
January: Afreen missed Ritu's housewarming. Salman didn't like her going to places "full of strangers", and it was easier to say she had a headache. She told herself it was one party.
March: Afreen stood in the shop holding two dupattas and texted Salman photos of both before buying. She planned what to say before he came home and read his mood from the way he shut the door. When Ritu called, she answered from the balcony in a whisper. "He's never hit me," she said, when Ritu asked if she was okay. "He just worries."
May: Ritu came over at lunch with biryani and a printed page from a women's helpline. Afreen read the list: checking plans with a partner, seeing friends less, fearing their mood. She had lived almost all of it. "I didn't think it counted without bruises," she whispered. That afternoon, with Ritu beside her, she called the helpline, and a counsellor talked her through what could come next.

qa.q: What did Afreen text Salman from the shop?
qa.a: Photos of both dupattas before buying.

qa.q: How was Afreen feeling by March?
qa.a: Afreen felt anxious and on edge, planning what to say and reading Salman's mood from the way he shut the door.

qa.q: What did Ritu do that helped?
qa.a: Ritu stayed in touch, brought food and a helpline page without blame, and sat beside Afreen while she called the helpline.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt hearing Afreen whisper from the balcony?
qa.a: Ritu likely felt worried and sad, sensing her friend's world shrinking, which is why she kept calling and later came with the page.
